name: Pierce v. Multnomah County
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Oregon)
topic: Force used on an arrestee in a jail after a warrantless arrest and before any judicial determination of probable cause; the Fourth Amendment, not the Eighth Amendment, governs; custodial detention for identification on a nonarrestable infraction; municipal policy
summary: A woman cited for boarding a train without proof of fare was handcuffed, taken to the county jail for a firm identification, and held about four hours, during which she said corrections officers yanked her arm behind her back, grabbed her hair, and forced her back into a cell after being told she was free to go. The jury was told to judge the force under the Eighth Amendment. The Ninth Circuit held that the Fourth Amendment sets the limits on the treatment of an arrestee detained without a warrant until the arrestee is released or found to be legally in custody on probable cause, so the Eighth Amendment instruction was error. It also held that a city policy of booking people for identification on nonarrestable offenses could be found unconstitutional.
coverage: The opinion was read in full, including Judge Rymer's partial dissent and all seven footnotes, from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/076/76.F3d.1032.93-35405.html.

The citation 76 F.3d 1032, the docket number 93-35405, the argument date of November 2, 1994, the decision date of February 14, 1996, and the panel (Fletcher, D. W. Nelson, and Rymer, Circuit Judges; Fletcher writing; Rymer concurring in part and dissenting in part) were confirmed from that file. The archive text does not print reporter page breaks, so references are to the opinion's numbered paragraphs as the archive presents them.
The trial record and the magistrate judge's rulings were not read; the facts are as the Ninth Circuit described them, including the plaintiff's testimony, which the defendants disputed.

The result on remand was not researched. Later Ninth Circuit and Supreme Court decisions on the standard for pretrial detainees (including Kingsley v. Hendrickson, which has its own brief in this library) were not reviewed for how they treat Pierce.
facts:
Stephanie Pierce, who represented herself in the Ninth Circuit, was stopped by a Tri-Met fare inspector as she boarded a train in Portland and cited for failing to produce proof of payment of fare. She had no identification, so the inspector called police to do an identification report. Pierce testified that when Officer Duncan of the Portland Police arrived she gave her name, date of birth, zip codes, addresses, and two phone numbers but refused to give her social security number. Duncan ran a radio check and found her name, a matching address, her driver's license number, and an arrest record. Pierce at first denied ever having been arrested, then confirmed a shoplifting arrest many years earlier (para. 2).

Duncan charged her with the misdemeanor of furnishing false information to a police officer and with the fare infraction. She was handcuffed and searched; she testified that Duncan did so in an excessively rough manner. She was driven to and led in handcuffs through a department store where Duncan went to question a shoplifter in an unrelated matter, then taken to the Multnomah County Detention Center for a "firm" identification. At the jail she was photographed, screened by a nurse, fingerprinted, searched, and placed in a cell (para. 3).

Pierce testified that during the roughly four hours she spent at the jail, corrections officers Karcher and Bowdle forcibly yanked her arm behind her back, shouted at her, grabbed her hair, and forced her back into a cell after she had been told she was free to go. The officers admitted applying "control holds" but said the force was necessary because Pierce was distraught, demanding, abusive, and uncooperative (para. 4).

At trial the City and Duncan stipulated that the false information charge was not the basis for the detention; they relied solely on the fare infraction (para. 6). The magistrate judge directed verdicts for the City and Duncan on the Fourth Amendment detention claim and for Bowdle on the claim that she seized Pierce after release. The judge instructed the jury on Eighth Amendment excessive force standards for the claims against Bowdle and Karcher, and the jury found for the defendants. Pierce had also inadvertently dismissed the County a month before trial and was refused leave to reinstate it (paras. 5, 7).
holding:
Reversed and remanded. Judge Fletcher wrote for the panel; Judge Rymer joined except as to Part I.

The Fourth Amendment governs force on a pre-arraignment arrestee. The defendants argued that the Eighth Amendment governs excessive force claims inside a jail. The court rejected that: the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on malicious or sadistic force does not apply "until after conviction and sentence," and because Pierce was detained merely for identification she was not subject to punishment, so the Eighth Amendment standard "is incorrect as a matter of law" (para. 32). Graham v. Connor had left open whether the Fourth Amendment continues to protect against excessive force after arrest ends and pretrial detention begins. Finding the Tenth Circuit's Austin v. Hamilton and the Second Circuit's Powell v. Gardner persuasive, and reasoning that the Fourth Amendment already governs the duration and justification of warrantless, post-arrest, pre-arraignment custody under County of Riverside v. McLaughlin and Gerstein v. Pugh, the court concluded it should also govern the conditions of that custody (paras. 33-35). "We hold, therefore, that the Fourth Amendment sets the applicable constitutional limitations on the treatment of an arrestee detained without a warrant up until the time such arrestee is released or found to be legally in custody based upon probable cause for arrest." The trial court erred by not directing the jury to apply Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness to the force used at the jail, and the verdict for Karcher and Bowdle was reversed (para. 36).

Officer Duncan's qualified immunity. The length and scope of a detention must be justified by the circumstances that authorized it. It was clearly established that once an officer has enough information to issue a citation, continued detention without probable cause to arrest for a crime is unreasonable (para. 15). Whether Duncan reasonably could have believed Pierce's identifying information was inadequate was disputed, so a directed verdict on qualified immunity was error; the issue was for the jury after both sides presented evidence (paras. 11, 19).

The City's policy. Pierce presented enough evidence of a City policy, practice, or custom of custodial detention for firm identification on nonarrestable offenses to survive a directed verdict, including an officer's testimony that he understood he could take an offender to the station for an identification check even when the offense carried no jail time (para. 23). Oregon's statute expressly denies authority to arrest for infractions, and Oregon courts strictly limit custody even for arrestable traffic offenses. "If the state has decriminalized conduct by denying the City and its officers the authority to arrest for a particular offense, then the City is acting unreasonably when it permits its officers to proceed as though they had the authority to arrest for the offense" (para. 28). An arrest is reasonable under the Fourth Amendment only if the officer has probable cause and is authorized by state or municipal law to make a custodial arrest for that offense (para. 29). The directed verdict for the City was reversed (para. 30).

Bowdle's seizure after release. A reasonable jury could find from Pierce's testimony that Bowdle had told her she was free to go, so that forcing her back into a cell was a new seizure; the directed verdict on that claim was reversed (paras. 39-40).

The County. Denying leave to reinstate the County, which had fully participated until it was inadvertently dropped a month before trial, was an abuse of discretion (paras. 43-46). The costs award was vacated.
dissent: Judge Rymer concurred in the result as to Duncan but disagreed with the majority's statement that Pierce's de facto arrest violated clearly established law, writing that whether Pierce had been adequately identified was a disputed fact and that was all that could be said on the record. She dissented as to the City, finding no evidence from which a reasonable factfinder could conclude that any City policy, practice, or custom existed; in her view the testimony of officers Kane and Pittock described practice at the county detention center and one officer's erroneous belief about the statute, not a City policy. She would have affirmed the directed verdict for the City (paras. 51-53). She joined the rest of the opinion, including the holding that the Fourth Amendment governs the force used at the jail.
notDecided:
Whether the force used by Karcher and Bowdle was excessive. The court held that the wrong standard was given to the jury and reversed the verdict. It made no finding on whether the control holds, the arm manipulation, or the hair grab were unreasonable; that was for a properly instructed jury on remand (para. 36).

Whether Duncan violated the Fourth Amendment. The court held only that disputed facts about the adequacy of Pierce's identification prevented a directed verdict on qualified immunity (para. 19).

Whether the City in fact had the policy Pierce described, or applied it unconstitutionally to her. The court held there was enough evidence for a jury; it did not find the policy proven (para. 30). Judge Rymer would have found the evidence insufficient.

Which standard governs after a judicial determination of probable cause. The holding is limited to arrestees detained without a warrant "up until the time such arrestee is released or found to be legally in custody based upon probable cause for arrest" (para. 36). The due process standard for pretrial detainees after that point, later addressed in Kingsley v. Hendrickson (which has its own brief in this library), was not before the court.
inPractice:
For jail and booking staff, Pierce answers a question that comes up every shift: which standard applies to force used on a person just brought in on a warrantless arrest who has not yet seen a judge. In the Ninth Circuit the answer is the Fourth Amendment. The force is judged by objective reasonableness, the same standard the arresting officer was held to on the street, from arrival through booking until the person is released or a judge finds probable cause. The Eighth Amendment's malicious and sadistic standard does not apply to anyone who has not been convicted.

The booking area is not a different legal world from the sidewalk. Control holds, arm manipulation, and placing someone back in a cell are uses of force to be justified by the circumstances: what the person was doing, what threat the person posed, what the security need was, and what lesser options existed. The officers here said Pierce was distraught, demanding, abusive, and uncooperative. A jury applying the Fourth Amendment will weigh that against what was done. Booking reports should be written with that in mind.

Release is a line. Once an officer tells a person she is free to go, a jury may treat forcing her back into a cell as a new seizure needing its own justification.

For patrol officers, once there is enough to write the citation, continuing to hold the person without probable cause for an arrestable offense is unreasonable, and taking a person to jail on an offense state law says is not arrestable can expose both officer and agency. Know which offenses carry arrest authority.
trainIt:
Dr. Sowards teaches Pierce in the custody standards line with Kingsley, Whitley v. Albers, Hudson v. McMillian, and Rodriguez v. County of Los Angeles. Pierce supplies the first segment of the custodial continuum the court described: arrest, then post-arrest but pre-charge or pre-hearing custody, then pretrial detention, then post-conviction incarceration. Teach the standards by segment. Arrest and warrantless pre-arraignment custody: Fourth Amendment objective reasonableness (Graham, Pierce). Pretrial detention after a judicial finding of probable cause: Fourteenth Amendment objective reasonableness with deference to facility policy (Kingsley). Convicted prisoners: Eighth Amendment good faith versus malicious and sadistic (Whitley, Hudson). In a mixed intake population, train everyone to the objective standard, because the newest arrivals are the ones to whom the Fourth Amendment applies.

Run booking scenarios with a distraught, verbally abusive, noncompliant arrestee held on a minor offense. Have officers articulate the Graham factors for each hands-on decision, the offense (here a fare infraction), the threat posed, and the resistance offered, and the reason a control hold or cell placement was proportionate. Then have them write it.

Train the release moment. Script the words used when a person is told she is free to go, and train that any restraint after that point needs a new, articulable reason.

Audit identification detention practices with the agency's legal advisor. The City conceded holding people for a mug shot even after an order to release for lack of probable cause, and the court said a policy of arresting for nonarrestable offenses could be found unconstitutional on its face.

Teach the posture. Pierce reversed a defense verdict for the wrong instruction and reversed directed verdicts. It did not find that any officer used excessive force or that the City's policy was proven.

The facts include the plaintiff's disputed testimony as the court recounted it. The result on remand was not researched. The holding on the governing amendment is limited to warrantless arrestees before release or a judicial probable cause determination; how later cases treat Pierce was not reviewed for this brief.

applications.title: Booking is still the Fourth Amendment
applications.body: In the Ninth Circuit, force on an arrestee held without a warrant is judged by objective reasonableness until the person is released or a judge finds probable cause. The Eighth Amendment does not apply to anyone who has not been convicted.

applications.title: Write the booking report like a street report
applications.body: Control holds, arm manipulation, and cell placement are uses of force to be justified by the offense, the threat, the resistance, and the alternatives. The officers here described the arrestee as distraught, abusive, and uncooperative; a properly instructed jury weighs that against what was done.

applications.title: Free to go means free to go
applications.body: Once an officer tells a person she is released, a jury may treat forcing her back into a cell as a new seizure that needs its own justification.

applications.title: Citation complete, detention over
applications.body: The court said it was clearly established that once an officer has enough information to issue a citation, continued detention without probable cause to arrest for a crime is unreasonable. Know which offenses carry arrest authority under state law.

applications.title: Teach the posture
applications.body: Pierce reversed a defense verdict for the wrong jury instruction and reversed directed verdicts. It did not find that any officer used excessive force or that the City's identification policy was proven.

quiz.q: Under Pierce v. Multnomah County, which constitutional provision governs excessive force used on a person arrested without a warrant and held in a jail before any judicial determination of probable cause?
options: The Eighth Amendment, because the force occurred inside a jail
The Fourth Amendment, until the arrestee is released or found to be legally in custody on probable cause
The Fourteenth Amendment's substantive due process shocks the conscience test
No constitutional provision; only state tort law applies
quiz.teach: The court held that the Fourth Amendment sets the limits on the treatment of a warrantless arrestee up to release or a probable cause determination, and that the Eighth Amendment does not apply before conviction and sentence.

quiz.q: What did the Ninth Circuit decide about whether officers Karcher and Bowdle used excessive force on Pierce?
options: It held their control holds were excessive as a matter of law
It held the force was reasonable because Pierce was uncooperative
It did not decide; it reversed the verdict because the jury was instructed under the wrong amendment
quiz.teach: The court reversed the jury verdict because the Eighth Amendment instruction was wrong as a matter of law. Whether the force was objectively unreasonable was left for a properly instructed jury.

quiz.q: What did the court say about taking a person to jail for a firm identification on an offense for which state law denies arrest authority?
options: It is always permissible if the person lacks a driver's license

A city policy permitting it could be found unconstitutional; an arrest is reasonable only if the officer has probable cause and is authorized by state or local law to make a custodial arrest for that offense
It is a matter of state law only and raises no Fourth Amendment issue
The court did not address the question
quiz.teach: Agreeing with the Seventh Circuit, the court said an arrest must be both supported by probable cause and authorized by state or municipal law to be reasonable, and that a city acts unreasonably when it lets officers proceed as though they had arrest authority the state has denied.
